overview.title: 📖 Overview: Resolving Old Dilemmas, Opening New Ground
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 7a–7b
overview.hebrewSource: שֶׁהַיּוֹצֵא מִן הַטָּמֵא — טָמֵא, וְהַיּוֹצֵא מִן הַטָּהוֹר — טָהוֹר
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf resolves yesterday's open question — does Rabbi Shimon's strict 'head and majority resembling the mother' standard apply to eating, or only to firstborn status? — before tackling a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua trade seemingly reversed positions on offspring of mixed parentage. From there the Gemara applies the mishna's 'follows the mother' principle to edge cases: a donkey's turbid urine, bee honey, and the membrane surrounding a newborn. A new mishna then asks what happens when one fish swallows another — and how we can tell swallowing from spawning.

slides.title: 🐫 Resolving Rabbi Shimon's Dilemma
slides.subtitle: Does 'head and majority' govern eating, or only firstborn status?
rows: A baraita mentions eating, then says 'if head and majority resemble the mother, obligated in firstborn status'
Rejected — the baraita simply shifts topics from eating to firstborn status; it proves nothing about the eating standard
A direct baraita: R' Shimon forbids a camel born of a cow, but if its head and majority resemble the mother, it becomes permitted to eat
Accepted — this proves Rabbi Shimon applies the same strict standard to eating as to firstborn status

callout.label: Conclusion:
callout.text: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ — Rabbi Shimon requires 'head and majority resembling the mother' in both areas; mere partial resemblance never suffices for him.

slides.title: ⚖️ 'This and That Cause It' — Mixed Parentage
slides.subtitle: A kosher mother, a non-kosher father: is the odd-looking offspring permitted?

lines.speaker: R' Yehoshua
lines.text: The offspring is permitted only if both parents are kosher of the matching kind — the plural 'seh kesavim, seh izzim' teaches: father a ram, mother a ewe.

lines.speaker: R' Eliezer
lines.text: No — the verse doesn't merely permit what's already obvious. It adds a case: a non-kosher-looking creature born to a kosher mother but sired by a non-kosher father is also permitted.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: But that's backward! Elsewhere, on a tereifa's offspring, Rabbi Eliezer is the strict one and Rabbi Yehoshua the lenient one!

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: Each follows his general rule except here, where this verse's unusual wording overrides it: R' Eliezer reads an extra 'seh' as leniency; R' Yehoshua reads the plural as stringency.

slides.title: 🐴 Rav Sheshet's Donkey Urine Dilemma
slides.subtitle: Turbid like milk, or merely water in and water out?

steps.content: 1️⃣ Question: is a donkey's urine forbidden like its milk? It's turbid, unlike horse or camel urine, which resembles plain water
2️⃣ First answer: the mishna says something emerges 'from (מִן) the non-kosher animal,' not merely 'out of' its body — a broader term covering any substance connected to it, including turbid urine
3️⃣ Challenge: but bees are non-kosher, and their honey is permitted! Not everything 'from' a non-kosher creature is forbidden

4️⃣ Resolved: honey is a unique Torah exception (Rabbi Ya'akov's reading of 'these you may eat') — bees merely gather nectar into their bodies, they do not produce it as a true bodily secretion the way milk or urine are produced

slides.title: 👶 The Birth Membrane: A Mere Secretion
slides.label: Rav Huna's ruling:
slides.hebrewSource: עוֹר הַבָּא כְּנֶגֶד פָּנָיו שֶׁל חֲמוֹר מוּתָּר... פִּירְשָׁא בְּעָלְמָא הוּא
slides.text: Rav Huna rules that the membrane emerging opposite a donkey's face at birth is permitted to eat, since it is 'merely a secretion' — not integral to either mother or offspring, and so unaffected by the donkey's non-kosher status. Rav Ḥisda cites apparent support: a baraita ruling the same membrane on a human newborn ritually pure, whether the baby is alive or dead. But the two disagree about exactly which combination the baraita means — both alive, both dead, or one of each — and the exchange ends good-naturedly, with Rav Huna conceding: 'if it is taught, it is taught,' and he cannot dispute an established baraita.

slides.title: 🐟 New Mishna: A Fish Swallows a Fish
slides.subtitle: Kosher and non-kosher fish found inside one another
rows: Non-kosher fish swallows a kosher fish
Permitted to eat the swallowed fish
It is simply a distinct kosher fish discovered inside — not the host's own offspring
Kosher fish swallows a non-kosher fish
It is 'not its growth' (אֵינוֹ גִּידּוּלוֹ) — the swallowed fish keeps its own non-kosher status regardless of its host

callout.label: The catch:
callout.text: Non-kosher fish spawn offspring while kosher fish lay eggs — so if no one saw the swallowing, the fish inside might be the host's own spawn. Rav Sheshet, Rav Pappa, Rav Naḥman, and Rav Ashi each explain, differently, how we can still be confident it was truly swallowed.

summary.principle: An offspring's kashrut and firstborn status consistently follow its mother — extended by the Sages to edge cases like a donkey's urine and a newborn's birth membrane — while Rabbi Shimon alone applies his stricter 'head and majority' standard to both eating and firstborn status alike.

flowSteps.content: 🐫 Resolved: Rabbi Shimon requires 'head and majority resembling the mother' for eating, just as for firstborn status
⚖️ Mixed-parentage dispute: R' Eliezer and R' Yehoshua each override their usual rule based on this verse's unusual wording

columns.content: 🐴 Donkey urine forbidden like milk — but bee honey is a unique Torah exception
🐟 New mishna: a swallowed fish keeps its own status, whether its host is kosher or not

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: 'That which emerges from the non-kosher is non-kosher' governs every edge case — except where the Torah carves out its own exception

quiz.q: How does the Gemara ultimately resolve whether Rabbi Shimon requires 'head and majority resembling the mother' for eating, not just for firstborn status?
o: It remains permanently unresolved
Yes — a baraita shows R' Shimon himself applies this standard: a camel born of a cow becomes permitted to eat only if its head and majority resemble the mother
No — any partial resemblance suffices for eating
The standard applies only to firstborn status, never to eating
quiz.e: A baraita citing Rabbi Shimon's own words proves that his strict 'head and majority' standard governs eating as well as firstborn status.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yehoshua's reading of the doubled, plural phrase 'seh kesavim veseh izzim,' what is required for a mixed-species-looking offspring to be permitted to eat?
o: Only the mother needs to be kosher
Both the father and the mother must be kosher of the matching species
Only the father needs to be kosher
The offspring's appearance alone determines its status
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehoshua reads the plural form as requiring that the father be a male lamb and the mother a female lamb — both parents of the matching kosher species.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara find the Eliezer/Yehoshua dispute about mixed-parentage offspring surprising?
o: Because they never disagree elsewhere
Because elsewhere, regarding a tereifa's offspring, their positions on 'this and that cause it' are reversed
Because Rabbi Eliezer never discusses kashrut
Because the mishna already resolved this case
quiz.e: Elsewhere Rabbi Eliezer holds the stricter position on 'this and that cause it' (forbidding a tereifa's offspring from the altar) while Rabbi Yehoshua is lenient — the opposite of their roles in this baraita.

quiz.q: Why might a donkey's urine be forbidden like its milk, according to the first answer given to Rav Sheshet's students?
o: Because donkeys are never permitted for any use
Because the mishna's language 'from (min) the non-kosher animal' is broader than 'out of' its body, and the urine's turbidity resembles milk
Because all animal urine is forbidden by Torah law
Because donkeys don't excrete urine at all
quiz.e: The mishna's phrase 'from the non-kosher' (rather than 'out of' its body) is read broadly to include any substance connected to a non-kosher animal, and donkey urine's turbid appearance (unlike horse or camel urine) resembles milk.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, if a kosher fish swallows a non-kosher fish, may the swallowed fish be eaten?
o: Yes, since it was found inside a kosher fish
No — it is forbidden because it is not the kosher fish's own growth, and it keeps its original non-kosher status
Yes, but only if it is digested first
The mishna does not address this case
quiz.e: The mishna rules it forbidden because the non-kosher fish is not the host fish's own offspring or growth ('אֵינוֹ גִּידּוּלוֹ') — its status as a distinct, non-kosher creature does not change.
